# Pain
Injuries hurt. Pain builds up from wounds, fractures, burns and other trauma, and fades slowly on its own once the cause is treated.
## Pain Levels - [bold]Aching[/bold] (mild): movement and aim are slightly impaired. - [bold]Hurt[/bold] (moderate): movement and aim are impaired, and actions take longer. - [bold]Agony[/bold] (severe): movement and aim are heavily impaired. - [bold]Pain shock[/bold]: the body is overwhelmed. The patient is badly slowed, keeps collapsing, and struggles to think straight.
The worse the pain, the slower you move and act and the more your aim sways. In pain shock you move at about 70% speed and actions take half again as long.
## Checking Pain - A health analyzer shows the patient's pain level and their [bold]shock risk[/bold]: how close they are to pain shock. - A trained medic can judge a patient's pain with a stethoscope.
## Painkillers Painkillers stop pain building up as fast, help it fade, and mask the symptoms. They don't treat the injuries underneath; stop the medication and the pain comes back. - [bold]Paracetamol[/bold]: mild. Takes the edge off. Overdose at 60u. - [bold]Tramadol[/bold]: a moderate opioid that strongly masks pain. Overdose at 30u. - [bold]Oxycodone[/bold]: a heavy opioid for severe pain that can fully mask pain shock. Overdose at 20u. - [bold]Fentanyl[/bold]: near-total pain relief, but a fatal dose is barely more than an effective one. Overdose at 10u. - [bold]Sleen[/bold]: a strong experimental painkiller. Overdoses turn toxic and disorienting. Overdose at 20u. - [bold]Soporific[/bold]: a sedative painkiller that causes drowsiness. At surgical doses it puts the patient to sleep. Overdose at 30u.
Strong painkillers or putting the patient to sleep are also important before surgery. See [textlink="Surgery" link="CMUGuideMedicalSurgery"].
